title: Resurrection and SafeHandle
cards/0/body:
A finalizer is an ordinary method, and this inside it is an ordinary reference. Store it in a static field, and the object is reachable from a root again. This is resurrection.

What happens then:

  • the memory is not freed: the object lives on, now in an older generation;
  • its entry has left the queues, so the finalizer will not be called a second time;
  • the objects it references may already be finalized (order is not guaranteed), so a resurrected object can be half torn down.
cards/1/q: A Zombie object was resurrected through Last. Later Zombie.Last = null ran. What happens at the next collection of its generation?
cards/1/options/0: The memory is freed, the finalizer is not called
cards/1/options/1: The finalizer is called again, and the object is resurrected again
cards/1/options/2: The object stays in memory forever: the GC leaves resurrected objects alone
cards/1/options/3: The process crashes: access to a finalized object
cards/1/explain: The finalizer has already run, and there is no entry in the finalization queue anymore. To the collector it is an ordinary object without a finalizer: unreachable means freed.
cards/1/wrong/1: For a second call the object has to be registered again through GC.ReRegisterForFinalize, and Zombie does not do that.
cards/2/body:
GC.ReRegisterForFinalize(obj) turns finalization back on: when the object becomes garbage again, the finalizer is called once more.

Together with resurrection this gives a "finalizer-based pool": in the finalizer the object returns itself to the pool and re-registers. Sounds thrifty, but in practice it is the worst kind of pool:

  • the object comes back only after a collection and a call on another thread, at an unknown moment;
  • every round promotes it and everything it references;
  • its fields may point at objects that are already finalized.

Pools are built explicitly: ArrayPool<T>, ObjectPool<T> and returning in Dispose.
cards/2/deep: In CoreCLR GC.SuppressFinalize sets a bit in the object header, and ReRegisterForFinalize clears it; if the queue entry is already gone (the finalizer has run), the runtime registers the object again. Hence a subtlety: re-registering "just in case" on a live object that still has its entry can produce a second entry and a double finalizer call. Call it only together with resurrection or after SuppressFinalize.
cards/3/explain: Pool.Add(this) puts the reference into a static collection, so the object is reachable from a root again. The next line resurrects nothing: it just turns the finalizer back on so the object returns to the pool next time too.
cards/4/body:
The Dispose pattern ends with a call to GC.SuppressFinalize(this). The resource is already released, the finalizer is not needed.

The finalization queue entry stays: the registration at new is already paid for. But the object is flagged, and when a collection finds it dead, it does not move it to the f-reachable queue but frees it right away. The savings: no call on the finalizer thread, no extra collection, no promoted graph.

Conclusion: a finalizer plus Dispose with SuppressFinalize is still more expensive than no finalizer at all. That is why a class holding a SafeHandle does not need a finalizer of its own.
cards/5/q: In a class with a finalizer, Dispose releases the resource, but GC.SuppressFinalize was forgotten. The user dutifully calls Dispose. What do we lose?
cards/5/options/0: Every object still goes through the f-reachable queue: an extra collection, promotion and a finalizer call
cards/5/options/1: Nothing: the GC can see Dispose was already called
cards/5/options/2: The resource is released twice and the process crashes
cards/5/explain: The collector knows nothing about IDisposable. Without SuppressFinalize the object is an ordinary finalizable one to it. If Dispose(false) is idempotent, there is no harm beyond the cost, but the cost is everything from the previous lesson.
cards/5/wrong/2: If the finalizer checks an "already released" flag, there is no second release. The loss is in performance.
cards/6/title: Why a bare IntPtr is not enough
cards/6/body:
A class keeps a handle in an IntPtr field and closes it in the finalizer. The Read method reads _h and passes the number to a native call. After the field is read, this is no longer used, and the JIT considers it dead.

If there are no other references, a collection can happen in the middle of the native call: the object is unreachable, the finalizer closes the handle, and Read is still using it. The old cure is GC.KeepAlive(this) after the call.

SafeHandle handles this itself: the wrapper object itself is passed to the call, the marshaller keeps it alive, increments its reference count before the call (DangerousAddRef) and decrements it after. Dispose in the middle of a call only marks the handle as closed, and ReleaseHandle runs on the last Release, exactly once.
cards/6/deep:
Another hole SafeHandle plugs: P/Invoke returned a handle, but it was not wrapped in time, because an exception happened between the return and creating the wrapper. For a returned SafeHandle the marshaller creates the wrapper object before the call, and after the call it only stores the number into it. That is why a derived class needs a parameterless constructor.

The counter and the "closed" and "disposed" flags live in one integer field, _state, and change through Interlocked. DangerousAddRef and DangerousGetHandle are available to you too, for when you need to pass the number to code the marshaller cannot see. Then DangerousRelease in a finally is mandatory.
cards/7/q: Once in a while Read returns an "invalid handle" error. Why?
cards/7/options/0: After _h is read nobody needs the Device object: a collection during Native.Read runs the finalizer, which closes the handle
cards/7/options/1: The finalizer is called before the constructor
cards/7/options/2: IntPtr gets boxed, and Read receives a copy
cards/7/options/3: Native.Open is called on the finalizer thread
cards/7/explain: The JIT tracks reference lifetimes up to their last use. this is used only to read the field; after that the object can become garbage even while its method is on the stack. The cure is SafeHandle instead of IntPtr, or GC.KeepAlive(this) after the native call.
cards/8/body:
SafeHandle derives from CriticalFinalizerObject. What this gives you now: if ordinary and critical objects became garbage in the same collection, the runtime first calls all the ordinary finalizers, then the critical ones. So a wrapper class finalizer can still flush its buffer through its SafeHandle: the handle itself is closed later.

Back then, in .NET Framework, "critical" meant more. The finalizer code was compiled ahead of time (CER, constrained execution regions) so it could not fail for lack of memory for the JIT, and it ran even on a rude AppDomain unload and thread abort. .NET Core has neither Thread.Abort nor AppDomain unloading, and CERs are not supported. What remains is the ordering guarantee and SafeHandle itself.
cards/8/deep: In the CoreCLR collector, critical finalizers sit in the queue as a separate segment, which is where the order comes from. The guarantee is weak: it covers only objects that died in the same collection. If the wrapper survived a collection while the SafeHandle died earlier (nobody else referenced it), the order is different.
cards/9/q: Match the method to what it does
cards/9/pairs/0/1: A collection frees the object without calling the finalizer
cards/9/pairs/1/1: The finalizer is called again when the object becomes garbage
cards/9/pairs/2/1: The object is reachable at least up to this line
cards/9/pairs/3/1: Wait until the finalizer thread drains the queue
cards/9/pairs/4/1: The handle is not closed until the matching Release
cards/10/body:
For a native resource without a ready-made wrapper, write your own SafeHandle. Most often you derive from SafeHandleZeroOrMinusOneIsInvalid: it already has IsInvalid for the values 0 and -1.

One thing is left: ReleaseHandle. The runtime calls it exactly once, from Dispose or from the critical finalizer. Inside: only closing the handle, no exceptions, locks or touching other objects. Return true if the release succeeded.
cards/11/q: Complete the wrapper for a native handle
cards/11/explain: The base class provides IsInvalid, the reference count and the critical finalizer, and the constructor with ownsHandle comes from it. Only ReleaseHandle is overridden: Dispose and the finalizer are already written in SafeHandle and will call it once.
